story_text.value:
I built a focused TUI tool for efficient parallelized tasks, early independent testers expressed 90%+ API savings and more direct results. This is accomplished by user smaller context windows, hybrid client-side compaction, tool compaction, and system nudges (to avoid polluting the base prompts).

My Shell features:

- Vim-inspired keybindings, your keys never have to leave the keyboard (some mouse control supported as well)

- Custom Markdown, LaTeX, and Mermaid rendering support

- On-demand subagents with LLM-directed context handoff

- Thread pooling, client-side compaction, tool compaction

- Supports Powershell without a degraded experience; also support VGA/VESA mode, run even when GPU drivers break!

- Single bundle, no external packages required

It’s opinionated, terminal-first, Vim-inspired; if that’s not for you, I have a web chat and a desktop app coming soon

story_text.value:
I'm Chris, and this is Zizq, a centralised job queue with a heap of awesome features I won't list off here.

https://github.com/zizq-labs/zizq

It gets through the queue fast under heavy throughput and requires no setup out of the box. The server is built in Rust as a single static binary, and it provides its own durable storage via an LSM tree storage engine (fjall), and aims to make searching and mutability of jobs first-class considerations. For example you can update jobs that are sitting in the middle of a queue without draining them and re-queueing them.

The server interacts with clients through a HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 API, using a persistent streaming connection with heartbeats and automated CI-tested disconnect or network partition/split detection, which acts as the liveness probe on both client and server. Because it's HTTP, clients are easy to write without re-inventing the queue machinery. Do it with curl and shell scripts on the command line if you really want to (I've actually done this but that is not released as I would strongly advise against doing such a thing in production). As of now there are four official clients, for Node, Rust, Elixir and Ruby. More to follow in due course and/or on request.

Jobs are always written to the LSM tree to ensure durability, but LSM trees are well optimised for write-heavy workloads like job queues (they always write sequentially) and internally Zizq employs some techniques like write coalescing and some lightweight use of in-memory skip list structures to get the most bang for buck out of the LSM tree storage.

Feedback and questions appreciated.

story_text.value:
This is a model that I made for a historical game. I wanted to have a 1:1 scale model of Europe, but my problem was that 100m data was too low-res while 10m LIDAR data was patchy, took hundreds of GBs to store and was full of manmade objects like mines, buildings and so on.

I trained this model on undeveloped landscape so that it can quickly add plausible erosion features, rocks, etc to the low-resolution height data and sort of reconstruct what the terrain would look like before any human interference.

story_text.value:
As I started to use `claude` and `codex` more it became too hard to manage all the sessions across all my tmux panes and sessions, so I built Puppet Master.

I see now there is quite a lot out there now for managing agents to write software, but

a) I started working on this before a lot of them, and b) there are things in Puppet Master that just don't exist all in one product.

For me I'd say the highlights are:

1) Web instead of terminal -- it's just a richer interface

2) iOS app so I can keep working on things from anywhere

3) Local + Remote workers (heterogeneous fleet), I work on things that are cross-platform and PM lets agents spawn across the fleet depending on workload needs.

4) Connections - first-class support for integrating MCP and REST API (ala OpenAPI definitions) into your agents. This goes above and beyond what a single harness can do via i.e an MCP integration. PM imports it (scoped to a bucket/project) and associates it to a policy. It lives between the agent and the remote MCP/API and enforces a policy. My normal flow is give full read access to agents and any APIs that do writes, approval needed. PM has native approval UI on web AND mobile so you can give real agency to your agents without being too permissive.

5) Code review interface is nice, 1-1 discussions on comment threads in the review, pretty responsive.

6) Forwards/artifacts allow agents to share static artifacts/html/etc,. OR serve up any dev server. This is proxied so even things on remote workers "just work" and you can access them, securely.

GitHub: https://github.com/chrismoos/puppet-master

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I posted AgentOS here a few months ago. Back then, it was pretty amazing to see what these agents can do and I'm improved it a lot since then.

The biggest change is that it's built for my phone now. I start work at my desk, walk away, and check on it or answer an agent from my phone over Tailscale. Chat sessions run in their own process, so restarting the server doesn't kill a turn that's halfway done.

It also runs tasks now. You give it a prompt, it makes a git worktree, the agent works there and opens a PR, and I review it later. Each workspace can have an orchestrator that starts tasks, reviews the PRs and merges the ones that pass CI and a review of that exact commit. Anything risky comes to me as an ask that needs Face ID to approve.

It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Aider, Cursor CLI, Amp and Pi. It's still free and all self-hosted.

npm install -g @saadnvd1/agent-os

https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os

I'd love feedback and as I'm sure there will be issues, please share them! Also, if you want to build your own, just fork it. It's all free.

story_text.value:
Author here. Bees is an agentic harness that runs on your own machine — macOS, Windows and Linux, MIT/Apache 2.0.

The problem we kept hitting in client work: every agent platform wanted to be the place your documents live. We wanted the opposite — the orchestrator reads your files in place, on your disk, and we never see them.

How it works: you describe work in plain English, Bees proposes the agents, stages, tools and schedule, and nothing runs until you apply it. Agents execute locally in their own run folders. A separate reviewer agent checks output before it advances a stage. Agents stop and ask for approval before external side effects like sending mail.

Coordination is deliberately thin. In a Regular org we sync team membership, process runs and stages, work claims, and file names with relative paths. Not contents. If you want no third party at all, pick a local model and local tools and it runs fully offline.

Model routing is BYO: local models, your own API keys, or the official Claude Code CLI you already have installed and signed into as yourself. We don't intermediate credentials and we add no per-token or per-run fee — that's the whole point.

Rough edges, honestly: {name the two weakest things — I'd lead with whatever your beta testers actually complained about}. Scripted installers exist but Linux distro coverage is the thinnest. Very happy to answer architecture questions, and I'd particularly like pushback from anyone running multi-machine setups.

Repo: https://github.com/Bees-bot/bees-desktop/

story_text.value:
A friend and I built this for our own calls and are sharing it as is. The itch: we kept copy-pasting Granola transcripts into Claude mid-call, and wondered what would happen if the agent just joined.

Two-minute demo: https://youtu.be/XhCSRiiL67A

How it works: a local Electron app joins the Meet in its own browser as a participant. Your agent drives it over MCP (or HTTP): tools to listen, speak, and write to a shared whiteboard. Any MCP agent works; we built for Claude Code first, and Codex and Cursor run it too. It is your actual session, on your machine, in your repo, with your skills, so it can do real work during the call instead of summarizing afterwards.

The hack: by default it does no speech recognition of its own. It reads Meet's live captions, and speaks through a virtual microphone. This is cheap and surprisingly good! (There is also an experimental realtime mode in app preferences that puts OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat, with your agent feeding it facts.)

Bring an ElevenLabs key for a better voice. Works with Google Meet and Slack huddles today; Zoom is in progress. Known issues are in the README.

Try it in your next Google Meet and surprise a friend. Let us know what you think!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nick. I'm a self-taught programmer with some B.S. in Applied Math, currently working construction but for the past few years have been building something that I think is extremely cool which is AA! My goal was to create a tool to hopefully help folks get jobs, and in the process perhaps gather and showcase job market data from a different perspective that I believe contains stories, ideas, and considerations worthy of sharing.

As of right now, AA has never successfully submitted anything, but I'm hoping that will all change very soon. Worst-case scenario users were my target audience with the goal being have it run efficiently, accurately, and reliably! I figured, if I could achieve something capable of functioning in this way then that would mean maximum availability to those who need it most.

- Customization Central Tons of ways to run: clone it, from a Flashdrive, inside Docker? Perhaps you only want it to collect qualified/aligned links or have it just apply to the links you provide or even Human in the Loop with set checkpoints? Avoid LinkedIn and Indeed and other login required sites, no problem!

- Download AA to a flash drive and plug it into a local library computer. I got the opportunity to work with my local library to offer folks sessions where they get AA up and running and while it does its thing they go and learn useful job skills and practice.

- Autonomy through Geometry: no hardcoded selectors anywhere. AA reads pages geometrically instead: Kuhn–Munkres assignment to optimally pair form labels to their inputs, convex hulls and VIPS-style segmentation for regions. Pure Python, deterministic, zero I/O, sitting behind ports.

As I mentioned, I made this to be a tool to help people find and get employed in this tough job market. Unfortunately, I knew this could only do so much which is why I tried to expand on that very idea!

- AA as a research instrument. Off by default; users can opt in, or withdraw, which deletes everything including the signing key. Zero PII collected, your profile can be encrypted with AES-256, the research data can be exported anytime, every row gets signed, and you can re-run any analysis and get byte-identical output.

- Biggest flaw to consider: once AA starts running, that device is dedicated to it until completion is reached or you end it early.

If this project caught your interest or attention there's a lot more to explore in my repo and would love for folks to go try and clone it and look around as I just pushed updates to hopefully make --install and --uninstall simple and non-destructive also use caution running session's as I was trying to impress a girl on Sunday and thought I'd try and show her my sick coding abilities and well within 6 seconds I managed to break absolutely everything which resulted in me saying saying wait every 2 minutes for 30 minutes until she left. Any who, if you are known as or even consider yourself one of the individuals below...

- Economist: What high-level things can I calculate for to have my data be more significant or applicable? What unique data could I gather that I may not consider insightful but is?

- Research Software Engineer: How bad is the damage? Any knowledge you can give me I would greatly appreciate!

- Mathematician: Sup nerd? Please look at my Math subsystem, Form Engine, Clingo code and tell me what to fix?

- Statistician: Checking out my signals_taxonomy.md would be dope and tell me the type of data I could perhaps report on that could be useful, beneficial, or applicable to current research?

- Lawyer: Would this perhaps get me in some bit of trouble?

- Any other kind of PhD person: Y'all are smart; if you're interested, ask me about my project in a way that relates to your field?

I'd love any feedback, input, suggestions, questionable insights, and funny insults that you'd like to toss my way!

title.value: Show HN: AA (a.k.a. AutoApply) – open-source job-hunt tool and research project

My goal was to create a tool to hopefully help folks get jobs, and in the process perhaps gather and showcase job market data from a different perspective that I believe contains stories, ideas, and considerations worthy of sharing.

As of right now, AA has never successfully submitted anything, but I'm hoping that will all change very soon. Worst-case scenario users were my target audience with the goal being have it run efficiently, accurately, and reliably! I figured, if I could achieve something capable of functioning in this way then that would mean maximum availability to those who need it most.

- Customization Central Tons of ways to run: clone it, from a Flashdrive, inside Docker? Perhaps you only want it to collect qualified/aligned links or have it just apply to the links you provide or even Human in the Loop with set checkpoints? Avoid LinkedIn and Indeed and other login required sites, no problem!

- Download AA to a flash drive and plug it into a local library computer. I got the opportunity to work with my local library to offer folks sessions where they get AA up and running and while it does its thing they go and learn useful job skills and practice.

- Autonomy through Geometry: no hardcoded selectors anywhere. AA reads pages geometrically instead: Kuhn–Munkres assignment to optimally pair form labels to their inputs, convex hulls and VIPS-style segmentation for regions. Pure Python, deterministic, zero I/O, sitting behind ports.

As I mentioned, I made this to be a tool to help people find and get employed in this tough job market. Unfortunately, I knew this could only do so much which is why I tried to expand on that very idea!

- AA as a research instrument. Off by default; users can opt in, or withdraw, which deletes everything including the signing key. Zero PII collected, your profile can be encrypted with AES-256, the research data can be exported anytime, every row gets signed, and you can re-run any analysis and get byte-identical output.

- Biggest flaw to consider: once AA starts running, that device is dedicated to it until completion is reached or you end it early.

If this project caught your interest or attention there's a lot more to explore in my repo and would love for folks to go try and clone it and look around as I just pushed updates to hopefully make --install and --uninstall simple and non-destructive also use caution running session's as I was trying to impress a girl on Sunday and thought I'd try and show her my sick coding abilities and well within 6 seconds I managed to break absolutely everything which resulted in me saying saying wait every 2 minutes for 30 minutes until she left. Any who, if you are known as or even consider yourself one of the individuals below...

- Economist: What high-level things can I calculate for to have my data be more significant or applicable? What unique data could I gather that I may not consider insightful but is?

- Research Software Engineer: How bad is the damage? Any knowledge you can give me I would greatly appreciate!

- Mathematician: Sup nerd? Please look at my Math subsystem, Form Engine, Clingo code and tell me what to fix?

- Statistician: Checking out my signals_taxonomy.md would be dope and tell me the type of data I could perhaps report on that could be useful, beneficial, or applicable to current research?

- Lawyer: Would this perhaps get me in some bit of trouble?

- Any other kind of PhD person: Y'all are smart; if you're interested, ask me about my project in a way that relates to your field?

I'd love any feedback, input, suggestions, questionable insights, and funny insults that you'd like to toss my way!
